name: AA Amyloidosis (Serum Amyloid A / Reactive Systemic Amyloidosis)

clinicalPearls: AA amyloidosis results from deposition of fragments of serum amyloid A, an acute-phase apolipoprotein whose hepatic synthesis is driven by interleukin-6, interleukin-1 and tumour necrosis factor during sustained inflammation.

It complicates chronic inflammatory disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, spondyloarthropathies and inflammatory bowel disease, and chronic infections including bronchiectasis, tuberculosis and osteomyelitis.
Hereditary periodic fever syndromes, notably familial Mediterranean fever, TRAPS and the cryopyrin-associated syndromes, are important and treatable causes, particularly in younger patients.
The kidney is the dominant target, with proteinuria progressing to nephrotic syndrome and chronic kidney disease as the usual presentation.
Hepatosplenomegaly, gastrointestinal involvement with diarrhoea and malabsorption, and less often cardiac disease may occur; macroglossia and periorbital purpura, characteristic of AL, are absent.
The circulating serum amyloid A concentration tracks disease activity and is the key monitoring biomarker; sustained suppression can halt or reverse amyloid deposition.

The therapeutic cornerstone is aggressive control of the underlying inflammatory drive, using interleukin-6, interleukin-1 or tumour necrosis factor blockade, with colchicine for familial Mediterranean fever.
Incidence has fallen substantially with improved control of chronic inflammatory and infective disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Persistent activation of the acute-phase response raises hepatic production of serum amyloid A, an HDL-associated apolipoprotein. When the circulating concentration remains chronically elevated, proteolytic processing yields amyloidogenic AA fragments that polymerise into fibrils and deposit in the extracellular space, with particular avidity for the renal glomeruli, interstitium and vasculature, as well as the liver, spleen and gut. Fibril accumulation disrupts tissue architecture and organ function, and the rate of deposition is broadly proportional to the magnitude and duration of the serum amyloid A elevation, so that suppressing inflammation can stabilise or regress disease. Individual susceptibility is modified by serum amyloid A isotype and other genetic factors, which explains why only a minority of patients with chronic inflammation develop amyloidosis.
additionalDifferentials: Diabetic nephropathy and other causes of nephrotic syndrome
Membranous nephropathy and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal subcutaneous fat aspirate or rectal or renal biopsy with Congo red staining and AA immunohistochemistry
Serum amyloid A and C-reactive protein to gauge inflammatory activity
Renal function and quantified proteinuria by urine protein to creatinine ratio
Serum free light chains and immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis
SAP scintigraphy to assess total organ amyloid burden
Genetic testing for periodic fever syndromes where clinically suspected
Targeted investigations to identify the underlying inflammatory or infective focus
redFlags: New nephrotic-range proteinuria in a patient with long-standing inflammatory disease
Persistently elevated serum amyloid A and C-reactive protein despite treatment
reference.prognosis: Outcome is largely determined by renal involvement and by the ability to suppress the underlying inflammation. Sustained normalisation of serum amyloid A can arrest progression and permit regression, whereas uncontrolled inflammation leads to end-stage renal disease.
pitfalls: Inferring the amyloid type from the clinical setting rather than confirming it by tissue typing, as AL can coexist with inflammatory disease
Failing to search for an occult inflammatory or infective focus
Not considering a hereditary periodic fever syndrome in younger patients
Relying on C-reactive protein alone when serum amyloid A is the more informative activity marker
references: Oxford Textbook of Medicine, chapter on systemic amyloidosis
Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology, chapter on renal amyloidosis
International Society of Amyloidosis nomenclature guidelines
management: Suppress the underlying inflammatory driver to lower serum amyloid A, using DMARDs and biologics including IL-6 and TNF inhibitors for rheumatoid and other inflammatory arthritides and definitive treatment of any chronic infection
Treat familial Mediterranean fever with colchicine and target other hereditary periodic fever syndromes with IL-1 inhibitors such as anakinra or canakinumab, or with TNF blockade, as appropriate
Manage renal involvement with control of proteinuria, RAAS blockade, treatment of oedema and general chronic-kidney-disease care
Provide renal replacement therapy for end-stage renal disease, with kidney transplantation considered once inflammation is controlled
Monitor serum amyloid A and C-reactive protein as biomarkers of disease activity, aiming for sustained suppression to arrest or reverse amyloid deposition
Offer genetic testing and counselling where a hereditary periodic fever syndrome is identified
Coordinate care between the relevant inflammatory-disease specialist, nephrology and a specialist amyloidosis centre
